oewn-00044347-n.learner: The act of getting rid of something, or the way you get rid of it.
examples: The town had to plan the disposition of all its old rubbish.

oewn-04657558-n.learner: The ability to enjoy funny things and to be funny yourself.
examples: She has a good sense of humour and can laugh at her own mistakes.

oewn-05612290-n.learner: In the Middle Ages, one of four liquids in the body that people believed controlled how a person felt in mind and body.
examples: Doctors in the Middle Ages thought too much of one humour could make a person sad or angry.

oewn-05404811-n.learner: Any of the liquids found in the body.
examples: The eye is filled with a clear humour that helps it keep its shape.

oewn-02283161-s.learner: In good condition and well made, so that it is solid.
examples: The old bridge is still strong enough to walk across.

oewn-00845738-s.learner: Firm and sure, done with force and without shaking or doubt.
examples: She gave a strong pull on the rope.

oewn-01829730-a.learner: Having a powerful effect on the body or on other substances.
examples: Wear gloves, because this cleaner is strong enough to burn your skin.

oewn-02536283-s.learner: So well protected that it cannot be attacked or secretly changed.
examples: Use a strong password so that no one can break into your account.

oewn-01162481-s.learner: Made by distilling rather than by fermenting, with a lot of alcohol in it.
examples: He drank a little beer but never touched strong drink.

oewn-01072383-s.learner: Fresh, because it was made or left only a short time ago.
examples: The hunters followed a strong trail into the woods.

oewn-01968612-s.learner: Of a verb, changing its form in a way that does not follow the usual rules.
examples: 'Sing' is a strong verb, because its past tense is 'sang'.

oewn-04810156-n.learner: The quality of being close to the real or correct value.
examples: The scientist checked the truth of her measurements on a second scale.

oewn-00811888-v.learner: To dodge a question or avoid answering it, or to take something for granted without showing it is true.
examples: He begged the point and started talking about something else.

oewn-01012145-v.learner: To say something strongly, as someone who has the power or right to say it.
examples: The general declared that no soldier would leave the camp that night.

oewn-00967903-v.learner: To make something known to the public, or to say it officially.
examples: The country declared war on its neighbour.

oewn-01012879-v.learner: To tell a customs officer about goods you are bringing in that you may have to pay tax on.
examples: Do you have anything to declare?
He declared the watch he had bought abroad.

oewn-02449420-v.learner: To give official approval for paying something out.
examples: The company declared a dividend of two dollars a share.

oewn-02305510-v.learner: In a card game, to choose the trump suit, or to choose to play with no trumps, by making the last bid of a hand.
examples: After the bidding was over, she declared spades.

oewn-02537291-v.learner: To test something to see how good it is, or to try it out.
examples: The engineers proved the new engine on a long drive before selling it.

oewn-00667548-v.learner: To show that something is true by a formal proof, as in mathematics.
examples: The student proved the theorem in just three lines.

oewn-01987148-v.learner: To grow bigger and take up more space.
examples: Leave the dough in a warm place to prove for an hour.

oewn-01979601-v.learner: To make something puff up by adding yeast or something that works like it.
examples: The baker proves the bread with yeast overnight.

oewn-00667689-v.learner: To get a court to officially accept a will as valid.
examples: The family had to prove the will before they could sell the house.

oewn-01748860-v.learner: To print a test copy of something so that it can be checked.
examples: The printer proved the page before printing a thousand copies.

oewn-00816521-a.learner: Happening at or near the start of a time or a series of events, or before the usual or expected time.
examples: Mr. Bennet was among the earliest of those who waited on Mr. Bingley.
Mrs. Bennet, through the assistance of servants, contrived to have the earliest tidings of it

oewn-00820993-a.learner: Being in, or happening in, the first stages of growing or developing.
examples: The illness is easier to treat in its early stages.

oewn-01733616-s.learner: Belonging to a time long ago.
examples: The early people of the island built their houses of stone.
Both sides are hoping for an early end to the war.

oewn-00823421-a.learner: Belonging to the first stage in the growth of a language or of its writings.
examples: This poem is written in Early Modern English.

oewn-00058666-r.learner: In an open and honest way, saying plainly what you mean.
examples: I asked her a simple question, but she would not answer directly.

oewn-07484465-n.learner: A running race that is one mile long.
examples: She won the mile at the school sports day.

oewn-13682724-n.learner: An old British unit of length equal to 6,080 feet (1,853.184 meters), which is 800 feet longer than an ordinary mile.
examples: By the old British measure, this nautical mile was 6,080 feet long.

oewn-13682973-n.learner: An old British unit of length once used for finding the way at sea, equal to 6,000 feet (1828.8 meters).
examples: British sailors once counted a sea mile as 6,000 feet.

oewn-13677032-n.learner: A unit of length used in ancient Rome, equal to 1,620 yards.
examples: The Romans set a stone beside the road at every mile.

oewn-13676880-n.learner: A Swedish unit of length equal to 10 kilometres.
examples: In Sweden a mile is ten kilometres, so the trip was only three miles.
